sources.locator: CS2023 Software Development Fundamentals; August 2023; section applicable to Decomposition
sources.claim: Decomposition divides one requirement into cohesive subproblems whose inputs and outputs connect and whose combined behavior covers the original need.

canonicalExplanation.summary: **Decomposition** means splitting one big requirement into smaller parts that each do **one clear job**, whose outputs feed the next part's inputs, and which **together cover everything** the original asked for. It's not about making many tiny functions — it's about clean jobs and clean hand-offs.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
"Build a quiz app" feels huge. Where do you even start? Break it down: a quiz application is separated into loading questions, presenting one question, checking an answer, updating score, and reporting the final result. Each part is small enough to write and test on its own, and together they cover the whole quiz. In this lesson you'll create and justify a decomposition whose parts cover the original requirement.

```predict
{"question": "The quiz must also show a timer. With parts load / present / check / score / report, is the decomposition complete?", "options": ["Yes, it's fine", "No — nothing covers the timer"], "answer": 1, "why": "A decomposition must **cover** the whole requirement. Missing parts mean missing features. Add a \"track time\" part."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Program, code and algorithm** and **Inputs, outputs and constraints**. Each part you create gets its own small input-output statement.

sections.heading: The model: jobs that connect and cover
sections.body:
| Part | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| load questions. | file name. | list of questions. |
| present question. | one question. | learner's answer. |
| check answer. | question and answer. | correct or not. |
| update score. | score and result. | new score. |
| report result. | final score and total. | message shown. |

Check three things: each part has **one job**, each output **connects** to the next input, and all parts together **cover** the requirement.

```reveal
{"prompt": "Would a part named `do_quiz_stuff` be a good piece?", "answer": "No. Its job is unclear, so you can't say what goes in or comes out. A good part's name says its one job."}
```

sections.heading: Too tiny is also a problem

includes: Split a requirement into cohesive parts with connected inputs and outputs.
Check that the parts together cover the whole requirement.

outcomes: Create and justify a decomposition whose parts cover the original requirement.

examples.title: Splitting a quiz app
examples.situation: A quiz application is separated into loading questions, presenting one question, checking an answer, updating score, and reporting the final result.
walkthrough: **One job each:** loading questions, presenting one question, checking an answer, updating score, reporting the final result.
**Connected:** loaded questions feed presenting; the answer feeds checking; the check result feeds the score update.
**Covering:** the loop over questions plus the final report covers the whole quiz requirement.
examples.result: Five cohesive parts that connect and together cover the quiz application.

examples.title: The monthly bill
examples.situation: Requirement: read this month's electricity units, calculate the bill with slab rates, add tax, and print a receipt.
walkthrough: Parts: read units → compute slab charge → add tax → format receipt.
Each output feeds the next: units → charge → total → receipt text.
Check coverage: every phrase of the requirement maps to a part.
examples.result: Four parts that together produce the receipt, each testable alone.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Decomposition means writing many tiny functions, even when their responsibilities and interfaces are unclear.
misconceptions.correction: Good decomposition creates parts with clear single responsibilities and well-defined inputs and outputs that connect and together cover the requirement. The number of functions doesn't matter; clarity of each job does.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Too tiny is also a problem", why didn't four one-line functions help?

analogy.example: Like a **restaurant kitchen**: one station preps, one cooks, one plates, one serves. Each has a clear job, passes food along, and together they deliver the full meal.
usefulFor: remembering one job per part and clean hand-offs
checking nothing is missing from the meal
limitations: Kitchen stations work at the same time; program parts often run in sequence.
In code you can test each station alone with fake inputs.

artifact: for q in questions: answer = present(q); score = update(score, check(q, answer))

steps.explanation: Loading questions produces the list the other parts will use.
Presenting, checking and updating score run once for each question.
Reporting the final result uses the finished score and the total.

remediation.explanation: Underline each verb in the requirement ("load", "check", "report"). Each usually becomes a part. Then draw arrows for what each hands to the next.

recap.summary: To create a decomposition, split the requirement into parts with one clear job each, make every part's output connect to the next part's input, and justify that the parts together cover the original requirement. Clarity matters, not function count.
